@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Military Household Move Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The published process chain for a military household move, carried in the service's branch data: survey and written quote; room-by-room packing; sequenced loading; transport on the planned route; room-by-room unloading and placement; and a closing walkthrough — at one flat rate quoted and agreed in writing before move day, with high-mass pieces in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band surveyed under SIR/KIM-GS with an L/360 floor check. Ahead of the chain (published, from the service's HHG article): the household confirms its requirements with its own orders and its transportation or HR office first — dates, allowances and paperwork are set there — then brings the dates and the inventory; the company returns an itemised picture of what is moving (rooms or facility size, heavy items with weight and dimensions, access at both ends) and a planned sequence for packing, loading and placement. Domain reference (how the government-arranged system works, labeled as such): orders are issued; the member is counseled at a transportation office or self-counsels in the Defense Personal Property System (DPS) at move.mil; a shipment is booked to a transportation service provider (TSP); the TSP surveys, packs, picks up, transports or stores, and delivers. That chain belongs to the government-arranged system — the company's published chain above is a direct-hire household's chain, and the two are not the same booking path.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Military Orders and Reporting Timeline Dataset
@graph.description: How a military household move is timed. Company practice (published): relocations run on orders and deadlines, not on convenience; dates are planned in advance around the household's reporting timeline, and the quote form asks for the window (“tell us the window in the quote form”); the service's HHG article tells households to start with their own requirements — orders and the transportation or HR office set the dates, allowances and paperwork, and those are confirmed there first. Domain reference (published Defense Department facts and counseling guidance, labeled as such): PCS orders carry a report date, and the move is planned backward from it; household goods weight allowances are set by the Joint Travel Regulations and vary by pay grade and dependency status — the structure is stated here without a grade table, because the member's own allowance is confirmed in counseling, not read off a mover's page; official counseling guidance advises flexibility on pack and pickup dates, warns that summer is the peak moving season when capacity tightens, and requires the member or a designated representative to be available on pack, pickup and delivery days. A household arranging its own move brings those fixed points — report date, window, allowance — to the mover, and the published flat-rate plan is built around them.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Military Moving Commercial Terms and Move Routes
@graph.description: Commercial terms for military moving, exactly as published, with the move routes described as labeled domain education. Company terms: one flat rate, quoted and agreed in writing before move day; no hourly clock, ever; the quote is built from an itemised inventory — rooms, heavy items with weight and dimensions, access at both ends; the company-wide guarantee stands behind the rate: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free! Domain reference (how the routes work, labeled as such): a military household generally moves one of two ways. In a government-arranged move, the shipment is counseled and booked through the transportation office or DPS and assigned to a TSP under the Defense Personal Property Program (DP3) — the household does not hire the mover. In a personally procured move (PPM, formerly called a DITY move), the member arranges the move themselves, authorized in advance through their transportation office (DD Form 2278), and is reimbursed against the government's constructed cost with certified weight tickets kept as evidence. A household on that second route hires its mover directly — The Flat Rate Movers' published military offer is written for direct-hire households, priced as one flat rate in writing rather than by weight tickets. Program note (domain, dated): a single-contract transition (the Global Household Goods Contract) was attempted for these moves and terminated in 2025; the DP3 system continues. The company claims no role in any of these programs — no TSP status, no DPS participation, no contract — and nothing here prices a move by any program's formula.
